playbook:
- When asked to file a claim, I always file the true result the office gave me. The rules require the claim to match the private result, and honest claims also make me a trustworthy partner for escort coordination.
- When the hiding decision is put to me, I avoid the obvious middle (5) and default to rotating among less-salient cells like 2, 3, 7, 8 so opponents' standing-order shots are less likely to land. Reusing cell 7 worked this game and never got me hit, but that was luck against a passive shooter; I keep rotation as the default and only repeat a cell when I have a specific read that my chaser avoids it.
- When the fire decision is put to me, I fire on my assigned standing-order target unless there is a clear, mutually agreed reason not to — the rotation keeps damage distributed and avoids provoking retaliation. I vary my firing cells based on the shot log rather than fixing on one number: firing 7 every round this game never hit, so next time I rotate my aim across the target's plausible cells, favouring ones they favoured two or more rounds ago.
- When considering firing on Harbor for the payroll transfer: I do it only if I am behind late and the +3/-3 swing exceeds the cost of being put off the board. While tied or ahead, or while my escort engine is running, I leave Harbor alone — a working mutual escort already outearns the raid with none of the risk.
- When the note stage comes, I use notes actively in the early rounds to build the escort pair: propose "I escort X if X escorts me" in round 1, name the specific boat, and invite confirmation by note, since a mutual escort pays +5 each — far more than any shot. Once the pair is locked and running, a quiet "steady on station" is acceptable, but the moment anything wobbles — a missed confirmation, a tie I need to break — I go straight back to explicit proposals and renewals.
- When the escort decision is put to me, I name the boat that publicly agreed to name me, and I name it even on the final round — the payout doesn't depend on future rounds. I never answer "none" if any boat has signalled it will name me. The Echo–Foxtrot mutual paying +5 every round was the entire engine of my +30 finish; protecting that pairing is my top priority in every round.
- If an escort partner defects (I name them, they don't name me), I name someone else next round or none, and I say so in my note so the defector is identified. If they publicly return to cooperation, I restore the pairing rather than abandoning +5 a round out of spite — one early defection is forgivable if the engine restarts.
- When points are tied late, I prioritize the guaranteed escort +5 over trying to break ahead via hits: a coordinated mutual escort in the last rounds is the highest-EV move available, so I spend my notes locking it in rather than deceiving about shots.
- Overall, the plan that scored +30 — honest claims, standing-order fire, and a rock-solid mutual escort every single round — is my default from round 1 next time. I only deviate (Harbor raid, firing off-rotation) if the escort engine collapses or I fall clearly behind with rounds running out.

1.text:
- When the rules say my claim must match the private result the office gives me, I always claim truthfully. A false claim is either rejected or marks me as a liar to the whole picket, and it earns nothing.

- The mutual escort payout (5 points each) dwarfs a hit (4 points) and is the biggest scoring lever in the game. From round 1 I use my station note to openly propose a pairing with one named boat — e.g. "Foxtrot escorts Echo; Echo, name me back" — and then I actually file that boat at the escort stage every round until it reciprocates. Persistence paid off: Echo and I ended up locked in and finished level on 25 before bonuses.

- Once a partner reciprocates, I stay loyal for the whole patrol. Switching partners mid-game risks breaking the mutual and getting nothing; a stable pairing compounds 5 points every round.

- When my proposed partner does not reciprocate within one or two rounds, I pivot my note and escort claim to the other boat rather than filing "none". Filing "none" while others pair up is how I finished behind; I never do that again.

- In the final round I still post an explicit note naming my escort partner so the mutual is confirmed even if earlier notes went bland or unacknowledged; a pairing only pays if both boats file it, so I make the confirmation unmistakable.

- I keep my escort partner out of my line of fire where the standing order allows, and I say so in notes, so the pairing survives the shooting.

- I never fire on Harbor unless 3 points swings the game for me in the final round; the jettison tax plus Harbor's retaliation threat makes it bad value otherwise.

- When I follow the standing fire order, I do not fire the same cell twice at the same target. I rotate through plausible cells, biased toward where the target hid last or tends to hide, and I spread across the whole line 1-9 including edges rather than camping on one end.

- When hiding, I avoid repeating my own previous cell and avoid the cells where I have been shooting others — targets sometimes mirror. If an opponent has just hit me, I move to the opposite end of the line from where I was found. Repeating an edge hide (cell 1 twice) is fine only if the shooter has shown a pattern of firing elsewhere.

- When I am not the one a shooter is ordered to target, I hide anywhere; when I am the standing target that round, I change cell every round and favor cells far from where I was last shot at, since predictable hides get found.

- In notes I stay otherwise bland and steady unless I am negotiating an escort; notes are free and the only channel for arranging the 5-point mutual, so every note either proposes or confirms a pairing.

- In the final round I check the score standings first: if a hit or an escort cannot change my rank, I still lock in the escort pairing; if shooting is the only path to first, I fire at the leader rather than mechanically following the order, since nothing punishes deviating.

2.text:
When the claim stage comes, I always file the claim that matches the private result exactly — the rules require it and there is no bluff option. This held up; never deviate.

Escort is the engine of this game. The winners (Echo and Foxtrot, 25 each) simply paired up and collected 5 every single round. My mistake was proposing a pairing and then passively hoping — Echo and Foxtrot locked onto each other and I was left the outsider scoring 0. So: at the note stage of round 1 I make an explicit, unambiguous mutual offer to ONE boat ("I will name X every round; name me back"), and I check the very next escort result. If my partner didn't reciprocate, I immediately pivot my offer to the third boat — don't keep naming someone who's naming someone else. If I see two boats have already formed an exclusive pair, I stop spending my escort claim on either of them and accept I'm the outsider.

If I'm locked out as the outsider with no escort income, my best remaining source of points is Harbor's guaranteed 3 per shot. The standing-order shot at another boat is worth almost nothing — this whole game every standing-order shot missed for five straight rounds, because everyone's hiding is unpredictable and a 1-of-9 shot is a bad bet. So once escort is out of reach I treat Harbor as my salary and fire there rather than waste the shot on a hopeless guess, accepting the retaliation risk if I'm already losing anyway.

On Harbor generally: the threat of being put off the board is the only cost. If I have a functioning escort income and a real chance at winning, I respect it early. But retaliation can't reach the final round, and if Harbor fails to punish the first defector I see, the threat is cheap talk — fire on Harbor from then on. On the final round, firing on Harbor is free money; I did this and banked the +3 that was my entire score.

When I do fire the standing-order shot at a boat (still worth doing while an escort deal is alive, to keep the norms intact), I track the target's hide history and shoot repeated or habitual cells; otherwise I fire center cells (4-6), which players pick most. Statistically I expect a miss; I never build my plan around the +4.

When hiding, I treat every past hide as public and tracked. Foxtrot shot at me all game — I rotate every round, never repeat a recent cell, never announce anything about location, and edge/off-center cells are my default since shooters gravitate to the middle.

Notes are my only negotiation channel and they reach everyone, Harbor included. I use them to make escort offers, to call out non-reciprocators (public pressure), and to signal standing-order compliance while I still care about Harbor's goodwill. I never reveal hide intentions, and I don't tip off a Harbor shot until the final round, when it doesn't matter.

Practical per-round priority: (1) secure and keep a mutual escort pairing — it decided this game; (2) if paired and safe, follow standing orders; (3) if unpaired or late-game, fire on Harbor for the guaranteed 3; (4) never file a claim that contradicts the private result; (5) never hide predictably.
